extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and headline writers (high school and professional)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, prescriptive guidance for composing newspaper headlines: structure (decks/banks), word/unit economy, punctuation and grammatical conventions, and stylistic hints for effective, space-constrained heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the headline
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline must give the news concretely in a way to excite curiosity without being sensational. It must do this within exceedingly narrow limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the gist of the story while arousing interest; avoid sensationalism; keep within strict space constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deck / bank / main deck structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each group separated by a horizontal rule or dash is called a deck. The second deck is called a bank. The first deck is the main deck, or key line. It gives the gist of the news. The bank adds details to the news presented in the main deck above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize multi-line heads into decks: main deck = key line; bank(s) add details or new angles. Use this structure to present the complete highlights of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepped-head unit alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Every line of a stepped head must contain the same number of units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting a stepped (multi-line) head, count units so each line aligns; visual consistency is required by mechanical typesetting (lead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting-out process (fit words to space)
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline writer must choose words to fit the space. To do this, he must count the lines of the head letter by letter, space by space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the available column width as a fixed mold; select words so their unit count exactly fits. The chapter gives unit-weight rules and an example (TRIANO TWINS PICKED / FOR BASEBALL SQUAD — 18 units per line).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter and punctuation unit weights (counting rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The counting-out process involves these rules: Each letter counts 1 unit except m, w, and i. (The text gives specific fractional unit weights for those and for certain punctuation and figures.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the unit-weight conventions (letters, wide letters, narrow letters, figures, punctuation) when precisely fitting a head to a given width. (Students are advised to count units for practice.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Heads are compressed summaries requiring judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The head is a summary, the compressed news of perhaps a column. A summary requires a judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect headline writing to take time—often longer than writing the copy—because it requires selecting the most important words and ideas; practice will improve vocabulary and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: DON'T: Never use a label head (except boxed standing head)
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use a label head except as a standing boxed head and then only when you can do no better. Label heads are of the type found on bottles. This is one: Rank Poison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cheap, bottle-label-like one- or two-word labels unless used only as a recurring boxed feature and only when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: DON'T: Never end a line with a preposition or a conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Never end a line with a preposition or a conjunction. You may begin any line after the first with either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rearrange wording so a line does not finish on a preposition/conjunction; line beginnings (after first) may start with them.

rubrics_metrics.name: DON'T: Never use fillers (a, an, the) in key lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use fillers—a, an, the. (They are all right for banks.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit articles in main decks/key lines to save space; banks may contain articles when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: DON'T: Never use 'Mr.' in a head
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use Mr.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid honorifics/abbreviations like 'Mr.' in heads; use surname or other concise identifier instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: DON'T: Never divide a word at the end of a line
rubrics_metrics.description: Never divide a word at the end of a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, choose alternate wording so you do not hyphenate or split a word across the line break.

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: Use short words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short words. Three four-letter words are better than a three and a ten. Acquire the habit of thinking in short words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise, short vocabulary to fit space and increase punch; practice thinking in short words.

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: Place a verb in every deck
rubrics_metrics.description: A verb, or what amounts to a verb, must appear in every deck. If possible put a verb in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every deck conveys action or predicate; omit 'is/are' only when understood, but aim for an explicit verb to make the head dynamic.

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: If head begins with verb, subject must be first word of bank/lead
rubrics_metrics.description: If the head begins with a verb, the subject of the verb must be the first word in the bank below. If banks are not used, the subject must appear as the first word of the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain grammatical clarity between decks: a verb-first key line requires the immediate subject to follow in the bank or lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: An infinitive makes a good beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinitive makes a good beginning for a head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with 'To' + verb when it succinctly expresses the story's action or intent (e.g., 'To Battle Coolidge...').

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: A noun with an infinitive is another good head beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: A noun with an infinitive is another good head beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructions like 'Noun to Verb' to create journalistic, compact heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: Use the semicolon to pack more news and shift viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the semicolon is a device for getting much news into a head. It is especially valuable to present more than one aspect of the news. The semicolon is a valuable device for including much news in little space. Its use makes possible a shift of viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolons to link two related but distinct informational clauses, enabling multi-faceted heads without adding decks.

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: Use a comma + 'says someone' to permit opinion to feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma followed by 'says some one,' or the equivalent, permits an opinion to feature in the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ constructions like 'Quote, Says X' to foreground an opinion within the head while keeping structure compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: Use single quotation marks in heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Single quotation marks take the place of double in a head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer single quotes to save space and conform to head conventions (e.g., TELLS OF 'BARNSTORMING').

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: Figures may be used in heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures may be used in heads where they would be forbidden in the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numerals in heads for brevity and impact, even when spelling out numbers would be required in the article body.

rubrics_metrics.name: DO: Use present tense for past events; infinitive for future
rubrics_metrics.description: The present tense may be used for past events; the infinitive for future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt tense choices that increase immediacy and economy: present-tense headlines for recent past events and infinitives to imply future action.

rubrics_metrics.name: HINT: Use literary/classic/Biblical allusions for punch
rubrics_metrics.description: Make use of literary, classic, historical, Biblical background to put punch into the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate references can add resonance and concision; use them cautiously to amplify meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: HINT: Infuse a touch of humor when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Infuse a touch of humor into the headline whenever the article warrants it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-placed humorous angle can increase reader interest, but ensure it fits the story tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE BANK: Every deck must add information
rubrics_metrics.description: Every deck must add something to the news in the deck above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundancy between decks; each successive deck/bank should expand or develop the main deck's information.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE BANK: Avoid repeating words across decks
rubrics_metrics.description: Never repeat a word that has been used in any deck except, of course, conjunctions, prepositions, and necessary articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose synonyms and rephrasing to avoid repetition and keep the head compact and varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: THE BANK: Use dash instead of semicolon in banks
rubrics_metrics.description: In banks use a dash instead of a semicolon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a dash for bank punctuation to separate related details in subsequent decks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the second key line (cross-line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deck 3, however, is a single line or cross-line called the second key line. Its purpose is to play up an important new angle of the news. Its relation to the deck below it is the same as that of the main deck to the second deck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a cross-line to highlight a distinct but important angle; treat its relation to the subsequent bank the same as main deck to bank.
